body.text: The US has slashed international development assistance to Southeast Asia. “America First” policies are leading to an approach to aid that is more transactional and deprioritises funding for gender equality, disability inclusion, and climate. Countries in turn are faced with two suboptimal outcomes: risk losing US funding entirely or sign new agreements while receiving far less than before.

The Trump administration’s elimination of the US Agency for International Development (USAID) has seen global US foreign aid spending fall 56.9% in 2025. We estimate these cuts have been far deeper in Southeast Asia, with a 76% decline in US assistance in 2025. The Lowy Institute’s 2026 Southeast Asia Aid Map also reveals that the US was reducing its foreign assistance to Southeast Asia even before the latest cuts.
The scale of the US cuts will stretch remaining development partners even further and leave large funding gaps where others do not step in.

The US is the largest grant donor in Southeast Asia, accounting for 23% of all grants to the region in 2024. The countries most reliant on US grants are particularly exposed. Almost all US projects in Myanmar and the Philippines have been terminated, leaving US$232 million and US$176 million gaps in their grant funding respectively.

Grants are growing more scarce as aid budgets shrink globally. The scale of the US cuts will stretch remaining development partners even further and leave large funding gaps where others do not step in.

Gender equality, disability inclusion and climate projects are areas where the US has historically been a major grant provider. Cuts have stemmed from removing “diversity, equity, and inclusion” programs, expanding restrictions on organisations involved with abortion to all global health assistance programs, and withdrawing from international climate agreements under the Trump administration’s “America First” policy agenda. In addition, the administration barred organisations receiving US foreign aid from promoting what it calls “gender ideology”, typically referring to rights for trans and non-binary people.
The US aid cuts will dramatically reduce donor support for key areas of good governance, basic health, and emergency relief (shown in the chart), accounting for almost half of all cuts.

The US has previously been the largest donor for democratic participation and anti-corruption organisations. The US cuts amount to more than 30% of total funding in these areas and risk a further narrowing of civic space in Southeast Asia. A further 23% of funding has been slashed for human rights bodies. Civil society organisations, already under pressure, stand to lose US$333 million, or 13%, of their total grant funding.

US cuts will also sharply hit total funding for key life-saving areas. US health sector funding cuts amount to almost 30% of total funding from all donors for reproductive health, basic nutrition, and family planning, as well as 18% of malaria control. It also accounts for 18% and 33% of total funding respectively for emergency food assistance and relief coordination and support services. With a strong El Niño already underway, these cuts will hit poorest households hardest and increase pressure on social protection systems already stretched by the impacts of the Iran war. This could increase the number of estimated deaths that the Centre for Global Development already attributes to US aid cuts.

The US cuts are not happening in isolation. Record reductions by 26 of 34 members of the OECD’s Development Assistance Committee in 2025 will add to the strain on Southeast Asia. Development partners providing stable support to the region are scarce and coordination among these donors will be essential. Regardless of whether other donors respond to the gaps, the US cuts and change in approach will have long-lasting consequences for how development aid works in Southeast Asia.

Dr Rahul Nath is a Research Fellow at the Lowy Institute’s Indo-Pacific Development Centre and is responsible for the Institute’s Southeast Asia Aid Map. His research areas include aid and development policy, development finance, sovereign debt, macroeconomic dynamics, multilateral development banks, and climate finance.

Taili Ni is a Research Associate in the Indo-Pacific Development Centre at the Lowy Institute, working on the Southeast Asia Aid Map. Her work focuses on tracking and analysing foreign aid and development finance flows to Southeast Asia.
